I laughed, then stopped. I had never seen him before.

His shop was narrow and dim, shelves crowded with pocket watches, cracked figurines, keys without locks. He reached beneath the counter and set out a green glass marble. “You swallowed one just like it when you were eight,” he said, then frowned. “No. Not this eight. The other one.”

My fingers hovered over the marble. It felt warm, as if it had been waiting in his palm for years.

“Who were you?” I asked.

He studied my face the way people study maps before taking the wrong road on purpose. “A ferryman,” he said softly. “And the river loved you enough to keep your name.”
